overview: This file traces the planning, construction, operation, and expansion of the Manchuria Chemical Industries Company’s chemical works at Dairen (modern Dalian) from 1932 through 1936. American consular reports describe the South Manchuria Railway Company’s decision to build an ammonium-sulfate plant in the Kwantung Leased Territory, its German technology and personnel, its closely guarded production methods, and suspicions that it could manufacture strategically useful chemicals such as ammonium nitrate and nitric acid. Later documents report the start of production, proposed aluminum sulfate, aluminum, caustic soda, and soda-ash facilities, and the rapid growth and geographical distribution of ammonium-sulfate exports, chiefly to Japan and Korea. Collectively, the papers place the enterprise within debates over Japanese-Manchukuo industrial relations, fertilizer markets, foreign machinery purchases, and preparations for war-related chemical production.

subfiles.title: Despatch on the proposed ammonium-sulfate plant at Dairen
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports confidentially the South Manchuria Railway Company’s decision to establish a large ammonium-sulfate plant at Dairen.
subfiles.summary: Vincent reports that the railway company has approved a Dairen plant with an announced annual capacity of 90,000 tons, using coal dust from Fushun, sulfur from Japan, and a nitrogen-fixation process resembling the Haber process. Baron Shiba asks that both the decision and his role as the source remain confidential. The choice of the leased territory rather than Mukden is presented as a response to Japanese opposition to competitive industrial development inside Manchukuo and as part of the wider debate over a Japan-Manchukuo economic bloc. Shiba argues that the plant would chiefly compete with British and German imports rather than established Japanese production.

subfiles.title: Departmental abstract of the 1934 Dairen chemical-plant report
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Abstracts a voluntary Dairen report about the construction and possible military purpose of the Manchuria Chemical Industries plant.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum states that Manchuria Chemical Industries, controlled by the South Manchuria Railroad, is building a large and highly secretive chemical plant near Dairen. Although nominally intended to manufacture ammonium sulfate and other chemicals, it is suspected of being designed to produce war chemicals. The abstract notes the employment of twenty-two German engineers and predicts that most fertilizer sales will be made in Japan because Manchurian demand is slight.

subfiles.title: Voluntary report on Manchuria Chemical Industries at Ganjingzi
subfiles.from: Arnold Van Benschoten, American Vice Consul at Dairen
subfiles.about: Provides a detailed commercial and technical survey of the new Manchuria Chemical Industries plant at Ganjingzi near Dairen.
subfiles.summary: The report describes the company’s ownership, capitalization, construction, labor force, planned capacity, markets, prices, manufacturing process, raw materials, and machinery. It records strong indications that the works could manufacture ammonium nitrate and nitric acid, notes elaborate secrecy measures, and identifies twenty-two German engineers working in restricted sections. The plant was expected to use the German Uhde process, coal from Fushun, pyrites from Japan, and equipment sourced largely from Germany, while detailed compressor specifications document its high-pressure installation. The report also emphasizes the lack of a local fertilizer market and the likelihood that output would be sold in Japan, China, and other overseas markets.

subfiles.title: Departmental memorandum on the start of chemical production
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Dairen despatch reporting that the new ammonium-sulfate works had begun operating.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reports production of ten tons of ammonium sulfate per hour at the newly completed Manchuria Chemical Industry Company plant. Initial output was to be exported entirely to Japan, with later entry planned into South China and South Seas markets. It also notes plans for aluminum sulfate, caustic soda, and soda-ash facilities.

subfiles.title: Despatch on the opening of the Ganjingzi ammonium-sulfate plant
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the start of production at Ganjingzi and related plans for aluminum, alum, caustic soda, and soda ash.
subfiles.summary: Grummon reports that the plant began operating on April 4, 1935, at one-third of its intended scale and was producing ten tons of ammonium sulfate per hour. Its first shipment, 800 tons aboard the Kojun Maru, left for Kobe on April 13; immediate output was destined for Japan, with later competition planned in South China and the South Seas. The despatch also describes negotiations for a large aluminum-sulfate plant capable of producing alum and aluminum for naval use, as well as proposed caustic-soda and soda-ash factories. The soda-ash project at Mukden was expected to threaten the trade of Britain’s Imperial Chemical Industries.

subfiles.title: Despatch on increased ammonium-sulfate output and exports
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Analyzes the rapid expansion of the Dairen plant’s ammonium-sulfate production and international exports.
subfiles.summary: Using customs statistics, Grummon shows that ammonium-sulfate exports from Dairen rose from 31,669 short tons in 1934 to 109,478 tons in 1935, with Japan by far the largest buyer. Korea and China also increased purchases, while exports to Hong Kong and the Netherlands Indies declined and those to the United States rose modestly. The despatch discusses discriminatory pricing, competition with soybean-cake fertilizer, and the limited appeal of artificial fertilizer to Japanese farmers. It concludes with plans to raise annual sulfate capacity to 240,000 tons and lists the Ganjingzi plant’s production of ammonium nitrate, nitric and sulfuric acids, benzol, pitch, tar, creosote, and coke.

interest: The file is unusually valuable because it combines diplomatic intelligence, commercial reporting, engineering detail, and trade statistics to document the emergence of a major Japanese-controlled chemical complex in Manchuria. The reports reveal how consular officers inferred possible military purposes from secrecy, German technical participation, high-pressure equipment, and planned production of nitric acid, ammonium nitrate, and naval aluminum. They also show the plant’s commercial logic and political sensitivity: it was located in the Kwantung Leased Territory partly to navigate opposition to industrial competition between Japan and Manchukuo, yet its production quickly transformed Dairen’s fertilizer exports. The machinery specifications, named contractors, source list, shipment details, and multi-year customs tables make the bundle particularly useful for historians of Japanese imperial industry, economic statecraft, technology transfer, and wartime mobilization.
